evidence.title: Tel Dan Stele
evidence.description: Aramaic inscription by an Aramean king (likely Hazael of Damascus) mentioning the 'House of David' and the 'King of Israel'.
evidence.significance: Earliest known reference to the House of David outside the Bible.

evidence.title: Zakkur Stele
evidence.description: Royal inscription of King Zakkur of Hamath and Lu'ash, describing his victory over a coalition led by Bar-Hadad of Aram-Damascus.
evidence.significance: Important source for Aramean political history and the Aramaic language.

evidence.title: Sefire Stelae
evidence.museum: Damascus National Museum / National Museum of Beirut
evidence.description: Three basalt stelae containing an Aramaic treaty between Mati'el of Arpad (Bit-Agusi) and Bar-Ga'yah of KTK.
evidence.significance: Longest known Old Aramaic inscription. Key source for Aramaic treaty language and diplomacy.

evidence.title: Tell Halaf Sculptures
evidence.description: Monumental stone sculptures including lions, sphinxes, and relief orthostats from the palace of Kapara, ruler of Bit-Bahiani.
evidence.significance: Major example of Aramean monumental art blending Syro-Hittite and Mesopotamian styles.

evidence.title: Hadad-yis'i Bilingual (Tell Fekheriye)
evidence.description: Bilingual Assyrian-Aramaic inscription on a statue dedicated to the storm god Hadad by an Aramean governor of Guzana.
evidence.significance: One of the earliest known Aramaic inscriptions and key evidence for early Aramaic script development.

evidence.title: Kilamuwa Stele
evidence.description: Royal stele of King Kilamuwa of Bit-Gabbar depicting the king in royal attire with a Phoenician inscription describing his achievements.
evidence.significance: Documents the political history of Bit-Gabbar and its relations with Assyria.

evidence.title: Panamuwa I Inscription (Hadad Statue)
evidence.description: Inscription in Samalian Aramaic on a statue of the storm god Hadad, erected by King Panamuwa I of Bit-Gabbar.
evidence.significance: Key source for the Samalian dialect and Aramean religious practices.

evidence.title: Panamuwa II Inscription
evidence.description: Funerary inscription in Samalian Aramaic erected by Bar-Rakib to honor his father Panamuwa II, who died during Tiglath-Pileser III's campaign against Damascus.
evidence.significance: Key source for the Samalian dialect and the political history of Bit-Gabbar.

evidence.title: Bar-Rakib Inscriptions
evidence.description: Multiple inscriptions of King Bar-Rakib of Bit-Gabbar, written in Imperial Aramaic rather than the local Samalian dialect.
evidence.significance: Among the earliest records using Imperial Aramaic, showing the spread of standardized Aramaic.

evidence.title: Katumuwa Stele
evidence.description: Funerary stele of a royal official named Katumuwa, with an Aramaic inscription describing mortuary rituals and the soul's dwelling in the stele.
evidence.significance: Unique evidence for Aramean beliefs about the afterlife and soul.

evidence.title: Kilamuwa Scepter
evidence.description: Inscribed scepter belonging to King Kilamuwa of Bit-Gabbar.
evidence.significance: Royal artifact demonstrating the material culture of Aramean kingship.

evidence.title: Hazael Booty Inscriptions
evidence.description: Ivory pieces inscribed with the name of Hazael, king of Aram-Damascus, found at the Assyrian provincial capital of Arslan Tash.
evidence.significance: Evidence of the wealth and reach of Aram-Damascus under Hazael.

evidence.title: Hazael Horse Frontlet
evidence.description: Bronze horse frontlet inscribed with the name of Hazael, king of Aram-Damascus, found at the Heraion of Samos.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramean diplomatic or trade connections reaching the Aegean world.

evidence.title: Melqart Stele
evidence.description: Basalt stele erected by Bar-Hadad, king of Aram, dedicated to the god Melqart. Contains an Aramaic inscription.
evidence.significance: Important evidence for Aramean royal dedications and religious practices.

evidence.title: Arslan Tash Amulets
evidence.description: Small limestone amulets with Aramaic incantation texts against demons and evil spirits. Found at the former Bit-Adini capital, then under Assyrian rule. Authenticity debated by scholars.
evidence.significance: If authentic, rare evidence of Aramaic magical and religious practices.

evidence.title: Arslan Tash Ivory Inscription
evidence.description: Inscribed ivory piece found at Arslan Tash (ancient Hadatu), capital of Bit-Adini after Assyrian conquest.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramean artistic production and luxury goods.

evidence.title: Til Barsip Wall Paintings
evidence.description: Polychrome wall paintings from the Assyrian-period palace at Til Barsip, former capital of Bit-Adini, showing military scenes and court life.
evidence.significance: Rare surviving examples of ancient Near Eastern wall painting from a site with Aramean heritage.

evidence.title: Hamath Inscriptions
evidence.description: Multiple stone inscriptions in Luwian hieroglyphs and Aramaic from the kingdom of Hamath, documenting its rulers.
evidence.significance: Shows the bilingual nature of the Hamath kingdom and Aramean cultural influence.

evidence.title: Hama Graffiti
evidence.description: Aramaic graffiti found during excavations at Hama (ancient Hamath), including short texts and names.
evidence.significance: Evidence of everyday Aramaic use in the kingdom of Hamath.

evidence.title: Tell Halaf Bit-Hilani Palace
evidence.description: Remains of a monumental bit-hilani palace with carved basalt orthostats, caryatid figures, and a scorpion gate.
evidence.significance: Best-preserved example of Aramean palatial architecture.

evidence.title: Tell Halaf Inscription
evidence.description: Aramaic inscription from Tell Halaf, destroyed during World War II bombing of Berlin.
evidence.significance: Lost artifact documenting Aramean presence at Guzana.

evidence.title: Bukan Stele
evidence.description: Aramaic inscription found in western Iran, one of the easternmost Old Aramaic texts discovered.
evidence.significance: Demonstrates the spread of Aramaic language and culture far beyond the Levant.

evidence.title: Neirab Steles
evidence.description: Two funerary steles with Aramaic inscriptions from the village of Neirab near Aleppo, depicting priests of the moon god.
evidence.significance: Important evidence for Aramean funerary practices and religious beliefs.

evidence.title: Tayma Stones
evidence.description: Aramaic inscriptions found at the oasis of Tayma in northwestern Arabia, dating to the Persian period.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic use in the Arabian Peninsula during the Achaemenid period.

evidence.title: Assur Ostracon and Tablets
evidence.description: Aramaic ostraca and clay tablets found at the ancient Assyrian capital of Assur, showing administrative use of Aramaic.
evidence.significance: Evidence that Aramaic was used alongside Akkadian in Assyrian administration.

evidence.title: Saqqara Aramaic Stele
evidence.description: Aramaic funerary stele found at Saqqara in Egypt, dating to the Persian period.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramean presence in Egypt during the Achaemenid period.

evidence.title: Elephantine Papyri
evidence.museum: Various (Brooklyn Museum, Cairo Museum, Bodleian Library)
evidence.description: Large collection of Aramaic papyri from a Jewish military community on Elephantine Island in the Nile, documenting administration, legal affairs, and daily life under Persian rule.
evidence.significance: Major source for Imperial Aramaic and daily life in the Persian Empire.

evidence.title: Hermopolis Aramaic Papyri
evidence.description: Eight Aramaic letters found at Hermopolis in Egypt, containing personal correspondence.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic-speaking communities in Egypt and their social networks.

evidence.title: Sarıaydın Inscription
evidence.description: Aramaic rock inscription in Cilicia (southern Turkey), dating to the Persian period.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic use in Anatolia during the Achaemenid period.

evidence.title: Daskyleion Steles
evidence.museum: Museum of the Ancient Orient, Istanbul
evidence.description: Aramaic funerary steles found at Daskyleion, the satrapal capital of Hellespontine Phrygia.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic as the administrative language of the Persian Empire in western Anatolia.

evidence.title: Luristan Aramaic Inscriptions
evidence.description: Aramaic inscriptions found in the Luristan region of western Iran.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic penetration into the Iranian highlands.

evidence.title: Kandahar Bilingual Rock Inscription
evidence.description: Bilingual Greek-Aramaic rock inscription of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, proclaiming Buddhist principles.
evidence.significance: Demonstrates Aramaic as a language of international communication reaching Central Asia.

evidence.title: Aramaic Inscription of Taxila
evidence.description: Aramaic inscription found at the ancient city of Taxila in modern Pakistan.
evidence.significance: Easternmost known Aramaic inscription, showing the language's reach to the Indian subcontinent.

evidence.title: Pul-i-Darunteh Inscription
evidence.description: Aramaic rock inscription of Ashoka found near Jalalabad in Afghanistan.
evidence.significance: Further evidence of Aramaic use in the Mauryan Empire's western provinces.

evidence.title: Bactria Aramaic Documents
evidence.description: Collection of Aramaic administrative documents from Bactria, dating to the late Achaemenid period.
evidence.significance: Shows Aramaic functioning as the bureaucratic language of the Persian Empire in Central Asia.

evidence.title: Aramaic Inscription of Laghman
evidence.description: Aramaic rock inscription of Ashoka found in the Laghman valley of Afghanistan.
evidence.significance: Part of the Ashokan edicts demonstrating Aramaic's role as a lingua franca in the East.

evidence.title: Palmyrene Inscriptions
evidence.description: Over 3,500 inscriptions in Palmyrene Aramaic from the ancient city of Palmyra, covering trade, religion, and civic life.
evidence.significance: Largest corpus of Aramaic inscriptions from a single site. Documents Aramean culture in the Roman period.

evidence.title: Aftuha Family Mosaic
evidence.description: Funerary mosaic depicting Aftuha and his family with a Syriac inscription.
evidence.significance: One of the earliest and best-preserved examples of Edessan Syriac art and epigraphy.

evidence.title: Orpheus Mosaic
evidence.description: Mosaic depicting Orpheus with a Syriac inscription naming the tomb owner and artist.
evidence.significance: Contains one of the earliest dated Syriac inscriptions known.

evidence.title: Funerary Inscriptions
evidence.description: Collection of Syriac funerary inscriptions from tombs around Edessa.
evidence.significance: Primary archaeological evidence for the language and culture of ancient Urhay.

evidence.title: Bethsaida Cultic Stele
evidence.description: A basalt monument depicting a stylized horned bull's head with a dagger, representing an Aramean deity (likely the storm god Hadad or a moon god). It was discovered broken near the monumental city gate complex.
evidence.significance: Provides vivid physical evidence of Aramean religious iconography, cultic practices, and political influence within the kingdom of Geshur.

evidence.title: Hazael Ivory Bed (Nimrud)
evidence.description: Inscribed ivory bed-head fragment bearing the name of Hazael, king of Aram-Damascus, found among the Nimrud ivories.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramean luxury goods reaching Assyria, likely as tribute or war booty.

evidence.title: Sam'al Citadel Gate Lions
evidence.description: Monumental basalt guardian lion sculptures flanking the citadel gate at Sam'al, capital of Bit-Gabbar.
evidence.significance: Major examples of Aramean monumental sculpture combining local and Syro-Hittite traditions.

evidence.title: Bar-Rakib Relief
evidence.description: Orthostat relief showing King Bar-Rakib of Bit-Gabbar seated on his throne before a scribe, with an Aramaic inscription.
evidence.significance: One of the best-known depictions of an Aramean king, showing court life and royal iconography.

evidence.title: Tell Fekheriye Statue
evidence.description: Full-size basalt royal statue of Hadad-yis'i, governor of Guzana, bearing the earliest known bilingual Assyrian-Aramaic inscription.
evidence.significance: Rare complete Aramean royal sculpture; key artifact for understanding early Aramaic script.

evidence.title: Bethsaida City Gate
evidence.description: Monumental four-chambered city gate complex from the Aramean kingdom of Geshur, with a high place and cultic installations.
evidence.significance: Best-preserved example of Aramean urban architecture in the southern Levant.

evidence.title: Ein Gev Inscription
evidence.description: Aramaic inscription found at the Sea of Galilee shore site of Ein Gev, within the territory of Aram-Damascus.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramean administrative presence in the Galilee region.

evidence.title: Behistun Aramaic Inscription
evidence.description: Aramaic version of the famous trilingual inscription of Darius I carved into the rock face at Behistun.
evidence.significance: Key Imperial Aramaic text demonstrating the language's official status in the Achaemenid Empire.

evidence.title: Wadi Daliyeh Papyri
evidence.description: Collection of Aramaic legal and administrative papyri from a cave in Wadi Daliyeh, left by refugees from Samaria.
evidence.significance: Important source for Aramaic legal language and Persian-period administration in the Levant.

evidence.title: Nabataean Inscriptions
evidence.description: Thousands of inscriptions in Nabataean Aramaic from the Nabataean kingdom, covering trade, religion, and dedications.
evidence.significance: Major corpus documenting a late Aramaic dialect that evolved into early Arabic script.

evidence.title: Hatran Inscriptions
evidence.description: Hundreds of inscriptions in Hatran Aramaic from the ancient city of Hatra in northern Mesopotamia.
evidence.significance: Documents a distinct Eastern Aramaic dialect and the culture of a major Aramaic-speaking city in Parthian Mesopotamia.

evidence.title: Dura-Europos Aramaic Texts
evidence.museum: Yale University Art Gallery / Damascus National Museum
evidence.description: Various Aramaic parchments, papyri, and inscriptions from the Roman-Parthian fortress city on the Euphrates.
evidence.significance: Evidence of multilingual Aramaic use in a diverse frontier community.

evidence.title: Dead Sea Scrolls (Aramaic texts)
evidence.museum: Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum, Jerusalem
evidence.description: Aramaic literary texts including the Genesis Apocryphon, the Book of Enoch, the Targum of Job, and the Testament of Levi.
evidence.significance: Major corpus of Jewish Aramaic literature preserving religious and literary traditions.

evidence.title: Samaria Papyri
evidence.description: Administrative Aramaic papyri from Persian-period Samaria, documenting sales, loans, and legal transactions.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic as the administrative language of the Persian province of Samaria.
